demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
María is thirty-eight, single, and lives alone in a small apartment near the industrial edge of the city. Six days a week she works the afternoon shift at a plastics factory, standing at a conveyor belt that never stops, fitting small caps onto bottles. The work is repetitive—her hands know the motion before her mind does—and she used to find a kind of peace in the rhythm. That was before.

Eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon just like this one, her supervisor pulled her off the line and led her to the break room. Her younger brother Carlos had fallen from a scaffold at a construction site. He was dead before the ambulance arrived. María remembers the break room’s fluorescent lights humming, the smell of burnt coffee, and the way her own voice sounded far away when she screamed. She could not stop screaming until a coworker held her shoulders and told her to breathe. Her boss drove her home. She sat on her couch in the dark for three days, not eating, not sleeping, not answering the phone.

Now, every afternoon when the hydraulic press in the factory slams down with a sharp thump, María’s body jolts as if an electric current has passed through her. She grips the edge of the conveyor belt, her breath shallow, until the moment passes. It happens dozens of times per shift. She has learned to hide it—turning away, pretending to stretch her neck—but her hands tremble for minutes afterward. The noise is not loud enough to be dangerous. It is only a sound. But to María it is the sound of Carlos’s body hitting concrete.

She no longer eats lunch with the other women on her line. She sits alone in a corner of the cafeteria with her back to the wall, scanning the room for exits. Two weeks ago, a coworker tapped her shoulder from behind to ask a question, and María spun around with her fist raised before she could stop herself. The woman backed away, eyes wide. Now nobody touches her. Nobody tries.

At night, she lies awake or does not lie at all. She walks from room to room in her apartment, checking the locks again and again, even though she knows nobody is coming. When she does sleep, she dreams of Carlos—not as he was, but as she imagines he must have looked after the fall. She wakes up gasping, sheets soaked through, his name caught in her throat. Some nights she stays awake on purpose, watching old cartoons on mute, because the dreams are worse than exhaustion.

She has stopped going to Sunday mass, stopped visiting her mother, stopped returning calls from her aunt. When the phone rings, her chest tightens so much she cannot breathe. She knows it is irrational—the news about Carlos came through a phone call, and now every ring feels like another death. Her mother’s voicemails pile up. María listens to them but never answers. She tells herself she will call back tomorrow. Tomorrow never comes.

At work, her performance has slipped. Twice last month she missed a defect in the caps because her mind had drifted to Carlos’s laugh, or the way he used to tap out a rhythm on her kitchen counter. Her supervisor has spoken to her gently, offering to move her to a quieter station. María said no. She does not know how to explain that the quiet is worse—that silence gives her room to replay the moment she heard the news, over and over, like a movie she cannot turn off.

She feels guilty for being alive. For not being there to grab his hand. For the fact that she screamed instead of staying calm. For the small, secret relief she felt when she realized she would not have to worry about his safety anymore—a thought that makes her hate herself.

María came to see me two weeks ago after her primary care doctor referred her. She sat in the chair with her coat still zipped, hands clenched in her lap, and said, “I don’t know why I’m here. I’m not crazy.” She has not missed a day of work. She has not cried since that first week. She has simply narrowed her world down to the path between her apartment and the factory line, and she is terrified that any expansion of that path will bring her closer to the moment she cannot escape.
